issue: The KV-budget segment contains several unexplained vertical white rules. They do not align with the eight 80 GB rank boundaries (which would fall at 80, 160, 240, … GB), and they do not correspond to the ~17 request slots derived in the equation. A reader can plausibly misread them as per-rank or per-request segmentation.
evidence: The bar is labelled 140 GB weights + ~64 GB runtime + ~436 GB KV budget. The vertical rules appear only inside the green KV segment and are evenly spaced from its left edge; the caption discusses aggregate rank feasibility but does not define these rules. The equation gives ~17.5 → ~17 requests, which does not match the visible number of segments.

figure: Figure 8.1 — Where inference computation and data movement actually live
issue: The vertical stack mixes execution resources with storage levels: 'tensor cores / ALU' is placed between registers and shared memory, and the right-hand arrow 'capacity grows / speed drops / distance grows' runs through it. Tensor cores are compute units, not a storage tier with capacity. The caption reinforces the conflation by saying the hierarchy runs from 'registers, tensor cores, on-chip SRAM' to HBM and interconnect.
evidence: The figure labels the tensor-core box 'arithmetic units' and maps 'matrix multiply' to it, while the capacity/speed/distance gradient applies to memory levels. The caption calls the vertical ordering a 'relative speed/capacity/distance ranking', but tensor cores have no capacity in this sense. A reader can incorrectly infer that data is stored in tensor cores or that tensor cores are a level of the memory hierarchy.
acceptance_test: Separate compute units from the memory hierarchy (e.g., place tensor cores/ALU in a side column or annotate them as execution resources), and make the capacity/speed/distance gradient apply only to storage levels. A reader should be able to state correctly that tensor cores are compute, not storage.

figure: Figure 8.1 — Where inference computation and data movement actually live
issue: The box label 'GPU interconnect host / multi-GPU' conflates host interconnect with GPU-to-GPU interconnect. The adjacent right-column text maps 'tensor/pipeline-parallel (TP/PP) communication' to this box, but TP/PP communication is GPU-to-GPU, not host traffic. Host-to-GPU traffic uses PCIe/NVLink C2C and is a distinct link.
evidence: The box reads 'GPU interconnect' then 'host / multi-GPU'. The caption says 'GPU interconnect' and 'other GPUs', and the right column says 'tensor/pipeline-parallel (TP/PP) communication'. A reader can incorrectly infer that TP/PP communication traverses the host link or that host traffic is part of the GPU interconnect.
acceptance_test: Relabel the box to distinguish GPU-to-GPU interconnect (NVLink/PCIe) from host interconnect, or add a separate host-link level. Verify that the TP/PP annotation points only to the GPU-to-GPU link.

figure: Figure 8.2 — Per-GPU roofline: dense FP16, one H100 vs one H200
issue: The H100 and H200 series are distinguished only by color (blue vs red), with identical solid lines and dot markers. In grayscale or for readers with color-vision differences, the two series can be difficult to tell apart. In addition, the 'decode batch=1' and 'decode batched' annotation lines point only to the H100 markers and cross the H200 line, so the labels can be misassociated with the wrong series.
evidence: The legend uses only color to distinguish 'H100 FP16 (3.35 TB/s)' from 'H200 FP16 (4.8 TB/s)'. Both series are drawn as solid lines with circular markers. The blue annotation line from 'decode batch=1' crosses the red H200 line near its marker; the 'decode batched' annotation similarly points only to the blue marker while the red marker at the same arithmetic intensity is unlabeled.
acceptance_test: Add a non-color distinction (dashed vs solid, different marker shapes, or direct labels on the lines) and reposition the decode/prefill annotations so they do not cross the other series. Verify the chart in grayscale and confirm that a reader can identify both H100 and H200 operating points without relying on color.
